newsitem.title: UK: UK stocks end off highs amid Wall Street jitters.
newsitem.headline: UK stocks end off highs amid Wall Street jitters.

text.p: A weak opening on Wall Street dragged UK stocks of their day's highs by the close on Thursday after a day in which the market continued to be gripped by nervousness following the share losses of recent sessions.
After rising 27 points at one stage, the FTSE 100 closed just 8.2 points higher at 3,990.7 British Gas, B.A.T and AB Foods were among the biggest gainers on year-end bargain-hunting.
With weak gilts also weighing on shares, traders said fears of a further shakeout in U.S. stocks were likely to hamstring the UK market for some time yet.
"I think the whole thing is very fragile and I think it's going to continue that way until things sort themselves out," said the head of equity trading at one major U.S. investment bank in London.
Gainers in the UK market were in a five-to-four majority and the Dow was down some 14 points as London closed.
The FTSE 250 index of mid-range stocks closed 12.7 points higher at 4,379.5 and the Reuters-HSBC 150 index was up 2.33 points, or 0.2 percent, at 1,079.50.

After tumbling on Tuesday by 53.2 points in its second major setback of the past week, shares initially took comfort from an in-line 0.1 percent rise in UK retail prices, easing fears of a near-term rise in interest rates.
The market extended its gains as U.S. Treasury bonds advanced following benign U.S. retail sales data.
Yet a weak early performance by the Dow revived anxieties following the volatile trading of recent sessions.
"Until Wall Street upset us we were doing alright," said one senior sales trader. "Wall Street is calling the tune and if it deteriorates further, we will do the same."
"It is very difficult to call this market short term, I think a certain amount of defensive action is being taken."
With a UK election due by next May and talk of a slowdown in U.S. company earnings growth, traders said there were plenty of reasons for investors to be taking profits on the gains seen during 1996.

"I think people will be locking in profits because of what may happen in the first quarter of next year," the sales trader said. The December long gilt future was down 21/32 at 109-5/16, with analysts blaming the decline on profit-taking and growing political jitters.
Trading volume in equities reached a modest 658 million by 1713 GMT, led by mobile 'phone group Orange, up 9-1/2p at 178-1/2 in volume of 25.2 million shares.
The stock was boosted by a newspaper report that mobile 'phone companies planned to raise the cost of calls from BT lines to their systems. Vodafone was up 3p at 249-1/2.
Tobacco and insurance conglomerate B.A.T was also active, up 6p at 494-1/2 in volume of 17.3 million, as continued demerger hopes helped fuel year-end bargain hunting.
Another target for bargain hunters was British Gas, in the throes of a demerger and a big underperformer this year.
Gas was up 15p at 233-1/2 in volume of 12 million.

Traders said much of today's blue-chip activity reflected investment funds rejigging portfolios at year-end. "There has been a lot of programme business and asset allocation changes and that is what is running the market at the moment," said the head trader at the U.S. investment bank.

Airtours rose 14p to 728-1/2, after a newspaper report that the company was poised for a 250 million acquisition spree, while pub operator Greenalls dropped 12-1/2p to 589-1/2, after profits towards the low end of analyst expectations.
A stock shortage squeezed Associated British Foods shares up 19p to 459-1/2, while London Electricity rose 12p to 652 amid a stock shortage after a better-than-expected dividend.
Baggeridge Brick plummeted 13p to 98-1/2 after posting a 47 percent drop in pre-tax profits.
-- David Holmes, London Newsroom +44 171 542 5106
